Archaeological Survey of India (ASI): history, circles and role

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is the national body for archaeological research and the protection of monuments, working under the Ministry of Culture. It was founded in 1861 with Alexander Cunningham as its first head. It protects more than 3,600 monuments of national importance through regional circles, licenses excavations and enforces the AMASR Act.

Talaash Heritage leads walks at ASI-protected sites such as Mehrauli and Purana Qila, and runs career sessions on ASI and museum work, arranged on request.

What is the Archaeological Survey of India?

The ASI is a government organisation, now attached to the Ministry of Culture, responsible for archaeological research and for protecting monuments and sites declared to be of national importance. It is headed by a Director General and has its headquarters in New Delhi.

Its work ranges from excavation and exploration to the conservation of monuments, the running of site museums, the study of inscriptions, the regulation of building near protected sites, and the nomination and management of World Heritage Sites. For most of the famous monuments people visit in India, from the Taj Mahal to Hampi, the ASI is the custodian.

History of the ASI: from Cunningham to today

Interest in Indian antiquities among British officials grew from the late 18th century, with the founding of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta in 1784 and the decipherment of Brahmi by James Prinsep in 1837. Alexander Cunningham, an army engineer with a deep interest in Buddhist sites, argued for a systematic survey, and in 1861 he was appointed Archaeological Surveyor. That year is taken as the founding of the ASI.

Cunningham used the accounts of Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang to identify ancient places, and his survey reports remain a valuable record. The survey was suspended for a few years, revived, and in 1871 Cunningham became its Director General. After uneven years at the end of the 19th century, John Marshall was appointed Director General in 1902 and reorganised the ASI, putting new emphasis on conservation and excavation. Under him, the excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro revealed the Indus Valley Civilization to the world in the 1920s.

Later Directors General included Mortimer Wheeler, who introduced more rigorous excavation and recording methods in the 1940s and trained a generation of Indian archaeologists. After independence the ASI expanded its work across the country.

How the ASI is organised: circles and branches

For managing monuments, the ASI divides the country into circles, each headed by a Superintending Archaeologist. There are about three dozen circles, and the number has grown over the years as new ones are created. Circles are usually named after their headquarters city, such as the Delhi, Agra, Bhopal or Hampi circle, and are divided into sub-circles. The circle is the office you deal with for permission to film or build near a protected monument.

Alongside the circles are specialist branches. These include excavation branches, the Epigraphy Branch (with headquarters in Mysuru) for inscriptions, a Science Branch for chemical conservation, a Horticulture Branch for gardens around monuments, and an underwater archaeology wing. The ASI's own training school is the Institute of Archaeology at Greater Noida.

The AMASR Act: how monuments are protected

The legal basis for the ASI's protection work is the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, usually called the AMASR Act. It allows the central government to declare monuments and sites of national importance, regulates excavation, and controls activities in and around protected places.

A 2010 amendment defined a prohibited area extending 100 metres from the limits of a protected monument, where new construction is generally not allowed, and a regulated area extending a further 200 metres, where construction needs permission. It also created the National Monuments Authority, which advises on permissions in these zones. Separate laws cover movable antiquities, notably the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972. State governments have their own acts for monuments of state importance.

What the ASI does, day to day

Most of the ASI's daily work is less visible than excavation.

  • Conserving and maintaining centrally protected monuments, more than 3,600 of them across India.
  • Exploring and excavating sites, and licensing excavations by universities and other bodies.
  • Running site museums at places such as Sarnath, Sanchi, Nalanda and Hampi.
  • Copying, studying and publishing inscriptions through the Epigraphy Branch.
  • Regulating construction and other activity near protected monuments.
  • Preparing nominations and managing many of India's UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
  • Publishing reports, including the annual Indian Archaeology: A Review.

Seeing the ASI's work for yourself

Every ASI-protected monument carries a blue board naming it as a protected monument under the Act. Once you notice them, you begin to see how much of India's built past is under its care. Check the ASI or site website for visiting arrangements before you go.

A walk through an ASI site with an archaeologist shows conservation choices in practice: original stone beside replacement, consolidated walls, excavated foundations. In Delhi, Mehrauli Archaeological Park and Purana Qila, where the ASI has excavated repeatedly, work well. For students considering a career there, our session on ASI, museums and public heritage careers explains recruitment, and the guide to how to become an archaeologist in India covers the routes. Questions people ask

Who founded the Archaeological Survey of India?

Alexander Cunningham is regarded as the founder. A British army engineer with a strong interest in Buddhist sites, he was appointed Archaeological Surveyor in 1861, the year taken as the founding of the ASI, and later became its first Director General in 1871.

What is an ASI circle?

A circle is a regional administrative unit of the ASI responsible for protected monuments in its area, headed by a Superintending Archaeologist. India has about three dozen circles, usually named after their headquarters city. Circles handle conservation, maintenance and local permissions for monuments in their jurisdiction.

What is the AMASR Act?

The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958, is the central law for protecting monuments and sites of national importance. Amended in 2010, it defines a 100-metre prohibited area and a further 200-metre regulated area around protected monuments, and set up the National Monuments Authority.

How many monuments does the ASI protect?

The ASI protects more than 3,600 monuments and sites declared to be of national importance. The exact number changes as monuments are added or, rarely, removed from the list. State archaeology departments protect thousands more monuments of state importance under their own laws.

Which ministry does the ASI come under?

The Archaeological Survey of India is an attached office of the Ministry of Culture, Government of India. It is headed by a Director General, with headquarters in New Delhi.
